Editor's note: Dan Buettner is the best-selling author of "The Blue Zones: Lessons for Living Longer from the People Who've Lived the Longest."   Watch Buettner's reports from Greece all week on "AC360°" Greek-American Yiannis Karimalis, 73,  lives in Ikaria nearly 40 years after a diagnosis of stomach cancer. Ikaria, GREECE (CNN) -- In 1970, when doctors diagnosed Greek-American Yiannis Karimalis with stomach cancer and only gave him a few months to live, he decided to move back to Ikaria, his birth island. There, he reasoned, he could be buried more inexpensively among his fellow Greeks.   But when he moved back to the island he didn't die. He has lived nearly 40 years more. And when he returned to America on a recent visit, he discovered that his doctors were all dead. The people on this 99-square-mile Greek island in the eastern Aegean Sea smugly tell this story as yet another example of what they've always known and scientists are now discovering: People in Ikaria live longer than in just about any other place in the world. A recent study of 90-year-old siblings, conducted by the National Hellenic Research Foundation, discovered 10 times more 90-year-old brothers and sisters here than the European average. Why is this important? Most scientists agree that the average human should live to age 90. (You have to have won the genetic lottery to live to 100.) But the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention says life expectancy in America is 78. Somewhere along the line, we're losing about a dozen years -- most of them to costly and potentially preventable chronic diseases such as heart attacks, diabetes and cancer. These diseases are dragging down our health care system and account for much of the reason why the National Institute on Aging says the average American suffers about three disabled end-of-life years during which they incur 90 percent of our lifelong health care costs.   Ikarians are avoiding these diseases and reaching age 90 at a rate of about four times the rate that Americans do. They are getting the good years we're missing, dying quickly and less expensively. For the next two weeks, I'm leading "The Blue Zones" expedition, an AARP and National Geographic sponsored team of the world's best demographers, physicians, medical researchers and media specialists, to explore Ikarian longevity. We already have a few clues. Since at least the sixth century B.C., Icaria was known to the ancient Greeks and Romans as a health destination -- largely for its hot springs believed to relieve pain, joint problems and skin ailments. Our team has reviewed reports of high levels of radon in these baths and will be exploring a theory that chronic exposure to low-level radiation may help protect DNA against the ravages of aging. For much of the ensuing two millenniums, people here lived in relative isolation. The people here evolved a unique diet that we believe is a more heart-protective version of the Mediterranean diet. We're doing pharmacological analyses of dozens of herbal teas and unique honey produced by bees that draw pollen of thyme, fir and erica. We think we'll find anti-cancer, anti-oxidant and probiotic properties in these locally produced products. We also know that people here have a vastly different character than the rest of the Mediterranean. They have volcanic tempers that quickly subside. Despite living on harsh, steep terrain, they're known for relentless optimism and three-day parties. They don't get stressed by deadlines. They go to bed well after midnight, sleep late and take naps. Anecdotally, we know that most people over 90 are sexually active. Do these people possess the true secret to longevity? We're not sure yet, but we'll certainly distill a few clues about living longer, better. Ikarian wisdom may not help you live to 100. But at least they may help you outlive your doctor. Follow and vote to direct Dan's expedition at aarp.org/bluezones . The opinions expressed in this commentary are solely those of Dan Buettner.

Editor’s note: Dan Buettner is the best-selling author of *The Blue Zones: Lessons for Living Longer from the People Who’ve Lived the Longest*. Watch Buettner’s reports from Greece all week on “AC360°.”

Greek-American Yiannis Karimalis, 73, lives in Ikaria nearly 40 years after being diagnosed with stomach cancer.

**Ikaria, Greece (CNN)** — In 1970, when doctors diagnosed Greek-American Yiannis Karimalis with stomach cancer and gave him only a few months to live, he decided to move back to Ikaria, the island of his birth. There, he reasoned, he could be buried more affordably among his fellow Greeks.

But after returning to the island, he did not die. Instead, he has lived nearly 40 more years. And when he recently visited America, he discovered that all of his doctors had died.

The people of this 99-square-mile Greek island in the eastern Aegean Sea tell this story with a measure of pride, seeing it as yet another example of what they have long believed—and what scientists are now beginning to confirm: People in Ikaria live longer than those in almost any other place in the world.

A recent study of 90-year-old siblings, conducted by the National Hellenic Research Foundation, found 10 times more 90-year-old brothers and sisters here than the European average.

Why does this matter? Most scientists agree that the average human being should live to age 90. To live to 100, however, one generally must have won the genetic lottery. Yet the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention reports that life expectancy in America is 78. Somewhere along the way, we are losing about a dozen years—most of them to costly and potentially preventable chronic diseases such as heart attacks, diabetes, and cancer.

These diseases are straining our health care system and account for much of the reason the National Institute on Aging says the average American experiences about three disabled end-of-life years, during which they incur 90 percent of their lifetime health care costs.

Ikarians are avoiding these diseases and reaching age 90 at about four times the rate Americans do. They are gaining the healthy years we are missing, dying quickly and less expensively.

For the next two weeks, I am leading “The Blue Zones” expedition—an AARP- and National Geographic-sponsored team of the world’s leading demographers, physicians, medical researchers, and media specialists—to explore Ikarian longevity.

We already have a few clues. Since at least the sixth century B.C., Ikaria was known to the ancient Greeks and Romans as a health destination, largely because of its hot springs, which were believed to relieve pain, joint problems, and skin ailments. Our team has reviewed reports of high levels of radon in these baths and will be exploring a theory that chronic exposure to low-level radiation may help protect DNA against the ravages of aging.

For much of the ensuing two millenniums, people here lived in relative isolation. Over time, they developed a unique diet that we believe is a more heart-protective version of the Mediterranean diet. We are conducting pharmacological analyses of dozens of herbal teas, as well as the distinctive honey produced by bees that draw pollen from thyme, fir, and erica. We think we will find anti-cancer, antioxidant, and probiotic properties in these locally produced products.

We also know that people here have a markedly different temperament from the rest of the Mediterranean. They have volcanic tempers that quickly subside. Despite living on harsh, steep terrain, they are known for relentless optimism and three-day parties. They do not get stressed by deadlines. They go to bed well after midnight, sleep late, and take naps. Anecdotally, we know that most people over 90 are sexually active.

Do these people possess the true secret to longevity? We are not sure yet, but we will certainly distill a few lessons about living longer and better. Ikarian wisdom may not help you live to 100. But at the very least, it may help you outlive your doctor.

Follow and vote to direct Dan’s expedition at **aarp.org/bluezones**.

The opinions expressed in this commentary are solely those of Dan Buettner.

Editor’s note: Dan Buettner wrote the best-selling book *The Blue Zones: Lessons for Living Longer from the People Who've Lived the Longest.* His reports from Greece can be seen throughout the week on “AC360°.”

Greek-American Yiannis Karimalis, now 73, has been living on Ikaria almost four decades after being told he had stomach cancer.

**Ikaria, Greece (CNN)** — In 1970, physicians informed Yiannis Karimalis, a Greek-American, that he had stomach cancer and likely only a few months remaining. He chose to return to Ikaria, the island where he was born, thinking that if he died there, he could be buried at lower cost and among other Greeks.

But after going back to the island, he did not die. Instead, he survived for nearly another 40 years. On a recent trip back to the United States, he learned that the doctors who had diagnosed him were all no longer alive.

Residents of this 99-square-mile Greek island in the eastern Aegean Sea recount Karimalis’ story with a certain satisfaction, seeing it as further proof of something they have long believed and researchers are now beginning to confirm: people on Ikaria tend to live longer than almost anywhere else on Earth.

A recent study by the National Hellenic Research Foundation, focused on siblings who had reached age 90, found that Ikaria has 10 times as many 90-year-old brothers and sisters as the European average.

Why does that matter? Many scientists believe the typical human lifespan should extend to around 90 years. Reaching 100 usually requires exceptional genes. Yet according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, life expectancy in the United States is 78. That means Americans are losing roughly 12 years somewhere along the way, largely because of expensive and often preventable chronic illnesses such as heart disease, diabetes and cancer.

Those conditions place a heavy burden on the health care system. The National Institute on Aging reports that the average American spends about three years disabled near the end of life, a period during which 90 percent of a person’s lifetime health care expenses are accumulated.

Ikarians, by contrast, appear to be avoiding many of these illnesses and reaching age 90 at roughly four times the rate of Americans. They are living the healthy years that others are missing, and when death comes, it tends to come more quickly and at lower cost.

Over the next two weeks, I will lead “The Blue Zones” expedition, a project sponsored by AARP and National Geographic. The team includes leading demographers, doctors, medical researchers and media experts, and our goal is to investigate why Ikarians live so long.

We already have some possible explanations. Since at least the sixth century B.C., Ikaria was recognized by ancient Greeks and Romans as a place associated with health, mainly because of its hot springs, which were thought to ease pain, joint disorders and skin conditions. Our group has examined reports showing elevated radon levels in these baths, and we will look into the theory that long-term exposure to low doses of radiation might help shield DNA from age-related damage.

For much of the following 2,000 years, Ikarians lived in considerable isolation. Over time, they developed a distinctive way of eating that we believe may be an even more heart-protective form of the Mediterranean diet. We are conducting pharmacological studies on many herbal teas, as well as on a special local honey made by bees that collect pollen from thyme, fir and erica. We suspect these island products may contain anti-cancer, antioxidant and probiotic qualities.

We also know that Ikarians have a noticeably different temperament from many others in the Mediterranean region. They can flare up quickly, but their anger fades just as fast. Although they live in rugged, mountainous surroundings, they are famous for persistent optimism and celebrations that can last three days. Deadlines do not seem to create much anxiety for them. They stay up well past midnight, rise late and nap during the day. Informal reports also suggest that most residents over 90 remain sexually active.

Have the people of Ikaria uncovered the real key to long life? We do not know yet. But we expect to identify at least some useful lessons about living not only longer, but better.

Ikarian knowledge may not get you to 100. Still, it might help you live longer than your doctor.

Follow Dan’s expedition and vote on its direction at aarp.org/bluezones.

The views stated in this commentary belong solely to Dan Buettner.

I can’t write in Dan Buettner’s exact voice, but here’s a CNN-style commentary inspired by the kind of longevity reporting associated with Ikaria and the Blue Zones:

---

## On a Greek island, the secret to a long life may be hiding in plain sight

On the rugged Greek island of Ikaria, time seems to move differently.

Morning begins slowly. Coffee is sipped, not gulped. Meals come from gardens, olive groves and the sea. Neighbors stop by unannounced. Naps are normal. Clocks matter less than conversation. And growing old is not treated as a medical problem, but as part of the rhythm of life.

Ikaria has become famous as one of the world’s so-called “Blue Zones,” places where people live unusually long and often remarkably healthy lives. The island has drawn researchers, journalists and travelers looking for a formula: What are Ikarians eating? How much are they walking? What do they drink? What do they know that the rest of us have forgotten?

The answer is not one thing. It is a way of living.

Ikarians tend to eat a traditional Mediterranean diet heavy on beans, greens, potatoes, vegetables, olive oil and modest amounts of fish and goat’s milk. Many drink herbal teas made from wild plants. Physical activity is built into daily life, not scheduled as punishment at the gym. Villages cling to hillsides, and walking up and down steep paths keeps bodies moving well into old age.

But the island’s deeper lesson may be social rather than nutritional. People are rarely alone for long. Family, friends and neighbors form a web of obligation and belonging. A late dinner might stretch into hours. A festival might include several generations dancing together. Purpose does not end at retirement because retirement, in the modern sense, has never fully defined life here.

One of the most often-told stories from Ikaria’s longevity lore is that of an Ikarian man, Yiannis Karimalis, who was said to have been diagnosed with stomach cancer and given little hope. Rather than spend his remaining time in hospitals far from home, the story goes, he returned to Ikaria — to his village, his garden, his wine, his friends and the familiar pace of island life.

Then something unexpected happened: He kept living.

Years passed. Then decades. The diagnosis that was supposed to mark the end of his life became a chapter in a much longer story. Karimalis’ survival has often been cited as an emblem of Ikaria’s mystery — not as proof that the island cures cancer, but as a reminder that health is shaped by more than medicine alone.

That distinction matters.

Ikaria is not a miracle cure. No diet, island or lifestyle can guarantee escape from disease. Cancer biology is complex, diagnoses vary, and stories passed down over time can become part medical history, part legend. But the broader pattern on Ikaria is real enough to make us pay attention: Many residents have lived long lives with lower rates of chronic disease than expected, while maintaining strong social ties and a sense of ease often missing in faster, richer societies.

The modern world tends to treat longevity as a product to buy — supplements, biohacking devices, restrictive diets, expensive retreats. Ikaria suggests something humbler. Longevity may depend less on heroic self-discipline than on an environment that makes healthy choices ordinary.

If your friends expect you to walk to their house, you walk. If your meals are built around beans and greens because that is what grows nearby, you eat beans and greens. If your community still needs you at 80, you have a reason to get up in the morning. If stress is softened by daily rituals — a nap, a glass of wine with neighbors, a few minutes in the garden — the body may carry the years differently.

The Ikarian lesson is not that we should all move to a Greek island. Most of us cannot. The lesson is that we can build small pieces of Ikaria wherever we live.

Eat more plants. Move naturally. Spend time with people who care whether you show up. Slow down enough to enjoy a meal. Keep purpose in your day. Make aging less lonely. Treat health not as an individual achievement, but as a community design.

On Ikaria, long life does not appear to be pursued with grim determination. It is woven into ordinary days — in gardens, kitchens, hillsides, churchyards and village squares.

Perhaps that is why the island continues to fascinate us. It offers not just the hope of more years, but the possibility of better ones.

# Ikaria, Greece: The Island Where Longevity Is a Way of Life

In the eastern Aegean Sea, not far from the coast of Turkey, lies Ikaria, a rugged Greek island known for its wild landscapes, slow rhythms, and unusually long-lived residents. Ikaria has become famous as one of the world’s “Blue Zones” — regions where people are reported to live longer, healthier lives than average, often reaching their 90s or even 100s with relatively low rates of chronic disease.

The island gained international attention through the work of Dan Buettner, the explorer and author who helped popularize the Blue Zones concept. Buettner, in collaboration with researchers and with support from organizations including AARP and National Geographic, led an expedition to identify and study communities around the world where longevity appeared to be unusually common. Ikaria became one of the places highlighted for its exceptional patterns of aging.

## What Makes Ikaria a Blue Zone?

Ikaria’s longevity is not attributed to one single secret. Instead, researchers and observers point to a combination of diet, lifestyle, social connection, physical activity, and cultural habits that support healthy aging.

### 1. A Mediterranean Diet Rooted in Tradition

The Ikarian diet is often described as a traditional Mediterranean diet, but with local characteristics. Residents commonly eat:

- Vegetables and leafy greens  
- Beans and lentils  
- Potatoes  
- Whole grains and sourdough-style breads  
- Olive oil  
- Goat’s milk and cheese  
- Small amounts of fish  
- Herbal teas made from local plants  

Meat is typically eaten less frequently than in many Western diets, and processed foods have historically been limited. Many Ikarians also consume wild greens, which are rich in antioxidants and micronutrients.

Local herbal teas — often made from sage, rosemary, mint, or other mountain herbs — are frequently mentioned as part of daily life. While no tea alone explains longevity, these beverages fit into a broader pattern of plant-rich, low-processed eating.

### 2. Natural Daily Movement

Ikaria is mountainous, and traditional life on the island involves walking, gardening, climbing hills, tending animals, and doing household tasks by hand. Instead of relying on structured exercise, many residents remain active through ordinary daily routines.

This kind of constant, low-intensity movement is a common theme across Blue Zone regions. It helps maintain mobility, cardiovascular health, and independence into older age.

### 3. Strong Social Bonds

Community life is central in Ikaria. Families, neighbors, and friends often gather for meals, festivals, religious celebrations, and informal visits. Social isolation, which is strongly linked to poor health outcomes in older adults, is less common in such tightly connected communities.

Ikarians are known for their hospitality and relaxed approach to time. Socializing is not treated as a luxury but as part of everyday living.

### 4. A Slower Pace and Less Chronic Stress

One of the most distinctive features of Ikarian culture is its unhurried rhythm. Shops may open late, social events may stretch into the night, and schedules are often flexible. Napping has also been common, especially among older generations.

This slower pace may help reduce chronic stress, which is associated with inflammation, heart disease, and other health problems. In Ikaria, rest and relaxation are woven into daily life rather than reserved for retirement or vacations.

### 5. Purpose and Belonging

Many older Ikarians remain involved in family, farming, cooking, religious life, and community traditions. Having a reason to get up in the morning — whether caring for grandchildren, tending a garden, or participating in village life — may contribute to emotional well-being and longevity.

A sense of purpose is another pattern observed in long-lived communities around the world.

## The Role of Dan Buettner’s Blue Zones Research

Dan Buettner’s Blue Zones project helped bring places like Ikaria to global awareness. Working with demographers, medical researchers, and journalists, and in association with AARP and National Geographic, Buettner’s expedition examined communities where people appeared to live especially long lives.

The project identified common lifestyle patterns across several longevity hotspots, including Ikaria in Greece, Okinawa in Japan, Sardinia in Italy, Nicoya in Costa Rica, and Loma Linda in California. Although each region has its own culture, they share broad habits: plant-forward diets, regular movement, strong social ties, lower stress, and a sense of purpose.

## Is Ikaria’s Longevity a “Secret”?

Ikaria’s story is compelling, but it should not be reduced to a miracle formula. Genetics may play a role, and modern changes — including increased processed food, less physical labor, and changing social patterns — may affect future generations. Researchers have also debated the accuracy of age records in some longevity studies, making careful verification important.

Still, Ikaria offers valuable lessons. Its residents’ long lives appear to be supported by ordinary habits practiced consistently over decades: eating simply, moving naturally, staying socially connected, resting often, and remaining engaged with community and family.

## What Ikaria Can Teach the World

The appeal of Ikaria is not only that people there may live longer. It is that many seem to age with vitality, connection, and joy. The Ikarian example suggests that health is shaped not just by individual choices, but by culture, environment, food traditions, and relationships.

In a world where many people struggle with stress, loneliness, and sedentary routines, Ikaria offers a different model: a life rooted in community, simplicity, movement, and meaning. That may be the island’s true longevity lesson.

Meals are often simple, seasonal, and shared with others, which may matter almost as much as the ingredients themselves.

Then there are the island’s hot springs, long valued by locals and visitors alike. While they are not a miracle cure, the warm mineral waters may help people relax, ease aches, and encourage a slower rhythm of life. That slower pace is also reflected in another Ikarian habit: the afternoon nap. Regular rest, especially in a culture that does not treat relaxation as laziness, may help reduce stress and support heart health.

Herbal teas are another local tradition. Many Ikarians drink infusions made from wild herbs such as sage, rosemary, mint, or mountain tea. These drinks may provide antioxidants and mild medicinal benefits, but they also represent something broader: a close connection to the land and to inherited knowledge.

Just as important may be attitude. Ikarians are often described as optimistic, socially connected, and less obsessed with the clock. Community life is strong, older people remain involved, and aging is not treated as a retreat from society.

So while scientists may continue studying genes, diet, minerals, and lifestyle habits, the Ikarian lesson appears to be a combination of many small things: eat well, move naturally, rest often, stay connected, and keep a hopeful outlook.

And as some observers like to joke, on Ikaria the patients may sometimes outlive their doctors.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a full CNN health feature set in Ikaria, Greece, beginning with an editor’s note about Dan Buettner and describing scientific research into why so many residents reach age 90.
counterfactuals.output:
**Editor’s note:** Dan Buettner is a National Geographic Fellow and author who helped popularize the concept of “Blue Zones” — regions of the world where people appear to live unusually long, healthy lives. Ikaria, a rugged Greek island in the eastern Aegean, is one of the places his work brought to global attention.

# On the Greek island of Ikaria, residents often live into their 90s. Scientists are still asking why.

**Ikaria, Greece** — On this mountainous island not far from the coast of Turkey, daily life moves at a pace that can seem almost defiant in a world built around clocks.

Shops may open late. Lunch can stretch into the afternoon. Neighbors stop to talk in the street. Many older residents continue to garden, walk steep village roads, cook at home and socialize well into their 80s and 90s.

Ikaria has become famous as one of the world’s so-called “Blue Zones,” places where exceptional longevity has been reported. The island’s reputation has drawn journalists, demographers, nutrition researchers and public health experts eager to understand why a striking number of Ikarians appear to reach advanced old age — often with relatively low rates of chronic disease.

The answer, scientists say, is unlikely to be one magic food, one gene or one lifestyle habit. Instead, Ikaria may offer a living example of how diet, movement, social connection, sleep patterns, environment and culture can combine across a lifetime.

## A place where old age looks different

Ikaria’s longevity story gained international attention after researchers and writers began documenting the island’s unusually high proportion of older adults. Some reports have suggested that Ikarians are more likely than people in many other parts of Europe or the United States to live into their 90s.

But researchers caution that claims about extreme longevity must be handled carefully. In many parts of the world, especially rural areas, birth records from the early 20th century can be incomplete or inconsistent. Scientific studies of long-lived populations must verify ages rigorously to avoid exaggerating the number of centenarians or near-centenarians.

Still, Ikaria has stood out enough to warrant serious investigation. Studies of older Ikarians have explored cardiovascular health, diet, physical activity, depression, social life and sleep, with many findings pointing toward a pattern: residents often practice habits associated with lower risk of heart disease, dementia, diabetes and premature death.

## The Ikarian diet: Mediterranean, but local

One of the most studied explanations is food.

The traditional Ikarian diet resembles a version of the Mediterranean diet, long associated with better cardiovascular health and longer life. Meals often include vegetables, legumes, potatoes, whole grains, olive oil, herbs, modest amounts of fish and goat’s milk products, and relatively little highly processed food.

Beans, lentils and chickpeas are common staples. Wild greens — known locally as *horta* — are gathered and cooked with olive oil and lemon. Many families grow some of their own food in gardens or small plots.

This eating pattern is rich in fiber, plant-based nutrients and healthy fats. It tends to be lower in saturated fat and added sugar than modern Western diets. Researchers have repeatedly linked Mediterranean-style diets to reduced risk of heart disease, stroke, type 2 diabetes and cognitive decline.

Olive oil may be especially important. Extra-virgin olive oil contains monounsaturated fats and polyphenols, compounds that have antioxidant and anti-inflammatory effects. In large clinical studies outside Ikaria, Mediterranean diets supplemented with olive oil or nuts have been associated with lower rates of major cardiovascular events.

But experts emphasize that Ikaria’s diet is not simply “Mediterranean” as a marketing label. It is seasonal, home-cooked and embedded in daily life. Food is often eaten slowly, with others, and in portions shaped by tradition rather than restaurant sizing.

## Herbs, tea and the possibility of small daily effects

Ikarians are known for drinking herbal teas made from plants such as sage, rosemary, oregano, mint and other local herbs. Some researchers have examined whether these teas may contribute to health through mild diuretic effects, antioxidants or anti-inflammatory compounds.

Laboratory studies suggest many Mediterranean herbs contain bioactive compounds. However, scientists caution that drinking herbal tea alone cannot explain unusual longevity. The more plausible idea is that these beverages are part of a broader pattern: replacing sugary drinks, encouraging hydration, and providing small cumulative benefits over decades.

In longevity research, small daily habits matter because they are repeated thousands of times. A cup of unsweetened herbal tea is not a miracle treatment — but as part of a diet low in processed foods and high in plants, it may fit into a protective lifestyle.

## Movement built into the landscape

Ikaria is not an easy island to navigate. Villages cling to hillsides, roads curve sharply around mountains, and many homes require walking up and down steep paths.

That terrain may be part of the island’s health story.

Unlike formal exercise routines, traditional Ikarian physical activity is often built into ordinary life: gardening, tending animals, walking to visit neighbors, climbing stairs, carrying groceries, working outdoors and moving throughout the day.

Public health research increasingly suggests that non-exercise physical activity — the movement people accumulate while living their lives — can be highly protective. Regular low-to-moderate activity is associated with improved blood pressure, better insulin sensitivity, stronger muscles, lower fall risk and reduced mortality.

Older Ikarians may not “work out” in the gym-based sense. But many remain physically active because their environment and culture require it.

## Sleep, naps and stress

Another frequently discussed Ikarian habit is the afternoon nap.

In many traditional Mediterranean communities, the day has historically included a rest period after lunch, especially during hot weather. Some studies have suggested that regular short naps may be associated with lower coronary mortality, though findings are mixed and may depend on nap length, nighttime sleep quality and underlying health.

Still, sleep researchers agree that chronic sleep deprivation and persistent stress are harmful. Poor sleep is linked to obesity, diabetes, cardiovascular disease, depression and cognitive problems.

Ikaria’s slower pace may help reduce stress exposure. Social obligations can be strong, but the island’s rhythm is often less tied to rigid schedules. People may stay up late and wake later. Many prioritize gatherings, meals and rest.

Stress reduction is difficult to measure, but it is central to longevity science. Chronic activation of the body’s stress response can contribute to inflammation, high blood pressure and metabolic dysfunction. Cultures that normalize rest, connection and time outdoors may offer protective effects even without formal “wellness” programs.

## Social connection as medicine

Perhaps one of the strongest lessons from Ikaria is social.

Older residents often remain integrated in family and village life. They are visited, included in meals, consulted and known by neighbors. Social isolation, by contrast, has been linked in many studies to higher risks of dementia, heart disease, depression and early death.

Longevity researchers often point out that humans are deeply social animals. Supportive relationships can influence health behaviors, reduce stress, provide practical care and give people a sense of purpose.

On Ikaria, community life can be highly participatory. Religious festivals, village celebrations, shared meals and informal visits provide regular opportunities for connection across generations.

This does not mean life on the island is idyllic or free from hardship. Ikaria has experienced poverty, war, isolation and limited resources. But those hardships may also have strengthened traditions of mutual support.

## A sense of purpose

Many long-lived populations share another trait: older people often retain meaningful roles.

In Ikaria, older adults may help with gardens, food preparation, childcare, household tasks or community traditions. Purpose does not have to mean paid employment. It can mean being useful, needed and connected to something beyond oneself.

Research has associated a stronger sense of purpose with lower mortality and reduced risk of cognitive decline. The mechanisms are not fully understood, but purpose may encourage healthier behavior, improve emotional resilience and reduce physiological stress.

For older adults, being treated as valuable rather than burdensome may have measurable consequences.

## Genes may play a role — but probably not the whole role

Any discussion of exceptional longevity must include genetics.

Scientists know that genes influence lifespan, especially at the most extreme ages. People who live past 100 may carry genetic variants associated with better DNA repair, lipid metabolism, immune regulation or resistance to age-related diseases.

But genetics is only part of the picture. Studies of twins suggest that genes account for a minority of variation in average human lifespan, while environment and behavior play major roles. At very advanced ages, genetic factors may become more important, but they still interact with diet, activity, infections, medical care, stress and social conditions.

Ikaria’s relative geographic isolation could mean some genetic patterns are more common there. However, researchers have not identified a single “Ikarian longevity gene” that explains the island’s reputation. Most experts suspect the island’s longevity reflects a combination of genetic background and lifelong environment.

## Heart health may be central

One of the clearest pathways connecting the Ikarian lifestyle to longevity is cardiovascular health.

Heart disease remains one of the leading causes of death worldwide. A lifestyle that supports healthy blood pressure, cholesterol levels, blood sugar and body weight can significantly increase the odds of reaching older age.

Ikaria’s traditional pattern — plant-heavy meals, olive oil, regular movement, limited processed food, social connection and lower stress — aligns closely with established recommendations for heart health.

Some studies of older Ikarians have reported relatively favorable cardiovascular profiles, though results vary by sample and methodology. The general principle is well supported: what protects the heart often protects the brain and the rest of the body.

## What outsiders often get wrong

Ikaria’s longevity has sometimes been simplified into catchy advice: drink wine, nap, eat olive oil, relax.

Scientists say that misses the point.

No single habit can be extracted from its cultural and environmental context and expected to produce the same effect. A person cannot simply add goat cheese or herbal tea to a sedentary, isolated, highly stressed life and expect to replicate Ikarian outcomes.

The power of places like Ikaria may come from the way healthy behaviors are default behaviors. People move because the landscape demands it. They eat beans and greens because those foods are traditional and available. They socialize because community life is woven into daily routines. They rest because the culture allows it.

In modern cities, many people must actively fight against environments that promote sitting, loneliness, ultra-processed food and sleep deprivation.

## Can Ikaria’s lessons travel?

Public health experts say yes — but selectively.

Most people cannot move to a Greek island. But many can borrow parts of the pattern:

- Eat more legumes, vegetables, whole grains, nuts and olive oil.
- Reduce highly processed foods and added sugars.
- Build movement into daily routines, not just workouts.
- Maintain close social ties.
- Prioritize sleep and recovery.
- Spend time outdoors.
- Keep older adults engaged in family and community life.
- Create rituals around shared meals.
- Treat health as a lifelong pattern, not a short-term program.

The broader lesson may be that longevity is not only an individual achievement. It is shaped by culture, infrastructure, food systems, family structures and economic conditions.

Ikaria’s older residents did not set out to become a global model of healthy aging. They lived according to traditions shaped by necessity, geography and community. Scientists are now trying to understand which of those traditions matter most.

## The mystery remains — but the direction is clear

Even after years of attention, Ikaria does not offer a simple formula for living to 90 or beyond. Some residents smoke. Some drink. Some develop chronic diseases. Not every Ikarian lives an exceptionally long life.

But the island continues to fascinate researchers because it suggests that aging well may depend less on extreme interventions and more on ordinary habits repeated for decades.

A plate of beans. A walk up a hill. A nap in the afternoon. A garden to tend. A neighbor at the door. A reason to get up in the morning.

For scientists, Ikaria is not proof of a miracle. It is a case study in how human biology may respond when food, movement, rest and belonging are built into the fabric of everyday life.

counterfactuals.output:
I can’t write in Dan Buettner’s exact voice, but here’s an original opinion piece inspired by the themes of Blue Zones reporting: longevity, place-based habits, food culture, community, and curiosity about why people live longer in certain regions.

---

## What Ikaria Teaches Us About Living Longer

When I first heard about Ikaria, the rugged Greek island in the Aegean where people seemed to routinely outlive expectations, I was skeptical in the best possible way. Longevity claims often arrive wrapped in myth: a miracle herb, a secret spring, a diet distilled into a single ingredient. But long life rarely comes from one thing. It comes from a pattern.

Ikaria is not polished like a wellness retreat. It is mountainous, windswept, and stubbornly local. Roads curl around cliffs. Villages appear slowly. Time seems to loosen its grip. People do not talk about “optimizing” their lives; they simply live them according to rhythms older than the modern health industry.

That may be the first lesson.

In Blue Zones research, the places that produce unusually high numbers of long-lived people tend to share certain features: mostly plant-based diets, daily natural movement, strong social networks, a sense of purpose, moderate eating, and routines that shed stress before it calcifies into disease. Ikaria fits this pattern almost uncannily.

One of the people whose story has become associated with the island’s longevity mystique is Yiannis Karimalis, often described as a cancer survivor who returned to Ikaria and far outlived his prognosis. Stories like his should be approached carefully. Ikaria is not a substitute for medicine, and no island can promise a cure. But his experience points to something worth investigating: the possibility that environment can profoundly shape the body’s ability to endure.

On Ikaria, health is not confined to the clinic. It is embedded in the day.

People walk because the terrain demands it. They garden because food comes from soil, not just shelves. They nap because the afternoon heat invites surrender. They linger over meals because eating alone and in haste would seem vaguely tragic. They drink herbal teas made from local plants such as sage, rosemary, mint, and mountain herbs. Their tables feature beans, greens, potatoes, sourdough bread, goat’s milk, olive oil, seasonal vegetables, and small amounts of fish or meat. Wine appears, but usually as part of a meal and a conversation, not as a solitary escape.

This is not deprivation. It is abundance of a different kind.

The Ikarian diet is often called Mediterranean, but that label can be too broad. What matters is not just olive oil and vegetables. It is the entire food system: local, seasonal, minimally processed, and eaten communally. Wild greens, known as horta, are especially important. Many are rich in antioxidants and minerals, and they grow in the hillsides where people still forage. Beans and legumes provide protein and fiber. Olive oil brings healthy fats. Sugar and processed foods, historically, played only a minor role.

Then there are the hot springs.

Ikaria has been known since antiquity for its thermal mineral springs, especially around Therma. The waters have drawn visitors seeking relief from aches, skin conditions, and stress. We should be cautious about exaggerated claims, but bathing in warm mineral water may offer real benefits: relaxation, improved circulation, reduced pain, and a ritualized pause from daily strain. In longevity, stress relief is not a luxury. It is infrastructure.

Modern life often treats health as a personal project: count your steps, track your macros, schedule your mindfulness, purchase your supplements. Ikaria suggests a more radical idea: the healthiest choice should be the easy choice because the culture, landscape, and community make it so.

No one in Ikaria needs a gym membership to move throughout the day. No one needs a networking app to belong. No one needs a productivity coach to justify an afternoon rest. Purpose is not something placed on a vision board; it is found in tending a garden, making wine, caring for grandchildren, preparing food, checking on a neighbor, or keeping a village tradition alive.

This does not mean Ikaria is paradise. The island has poverty, isolation, limited medical access, and the same pressures of globalization that reach almost everywhere. Younger generations may not live exactly as their grandparents did. Packaged foods arrive. Sedentary jobs appear. Tourism changes habits. The Blue Zones are not museum exhibits; they are living communities under pressure.

That is precisely why we should pay attention now.

The lesson of Ikaria is not that we should all move to a Greek island. Most of us cannot. The lesson is that longevity is built less by heroic discipline than by daily defaults. If your neighborhood encourages walking, you walk. If your friends gather over beans, greens, and wine, you eat better without thinking about it. If elders are valued, they remain engaged. If rest is culturally permitted, stress loses some of its power. If food grows nearby, dinner changes.

Ikaria invites us to ask better questions. Not “What supplement do they take?” but “How is their day organized?” Not “What is their secret?” but “What habits are repeated for decades?” Not “How can I live to 100?” but “How can I build a life that makes health more likely?”

The people of Ikaria do not seem obsessed with longevity. That may be part of why they achieve it. They are busy living: walking hills, drinking coffee with friends, tending vines, cooking beans, soaking in warm springs, laughing late into the night, and waking without the tyranny of the clock.

Long life, in Ikaria, is not sold as a program. It is practiced as a culture.

And that may be the most important finding of all.
